rationale: B wins because it found the reportable pressure point in the update: "The installer bottleneck: a home battery that claims it skips the rewiring." That is a falsifiable beat story with a protagonist, a call list, and proof requirements. A is competent, but "The power-bank company just built a whole-home battery" and "Why a phone-charger giant is betting on home energy storage" are two suits on the same brand-extension mannequin.
gaps_in_A: "confirmation from Anker or an installer partner of what \"installs without major electrical rewiring\" means in practice" buries the strongest supplied claim as proof support instead of making it the angle.

"The power-bank company just built a whole-home battery" and "Why a phone-charger giant is betting on home energy storage" are too close. One is brand trust, one is corporate strategy, but both ask reporters to care that Anker moved upmarket.
"Story type: category-creation" is inflated. Anker is entering an existing home-battery market; the story is category stretch or channel strategy, not a new category.
"Anker naming Tesla Powerwall as direct competition" is a shade too confident. The update says it competes with Tesla Powerwall; it does not say Anker named Tesla.
gaps_in_B: "who is allowed to sell into the home electrical panel" imports a permissions/regulatory frame the update did not supply.
"Soft costs and electrician scarcity are the recurring problem in that beat" may be true, but it is outside the given facts and needs a source if it is used as the why-care.

"when a competing product is actually on sale in the US" overstates the launch facts. The update says US launch; pricing, installer network, and capacity are only partially disclosed, so availability is not nailed down.
"Next step: `newsjack-detector`" is a little workflow-drunk. For this launch, the immediate move is to lock price/capacity/warranty/installer proof and fit-check the installer angle.
